quizzes.title: Key terms and ideas
quizzes.intro: Ten quick checks on loom output, A-grade and yarn for an order.

questions.q: Inches of cloth per minute are rpm × efficiency ÷ PPI because
options: each revolution inserts one pick and each pick adds 1 ÷ PPI inch of cloth
the reed moves one inch per pick
the loom runs 60 minutes an hour
questions.explain: At 800 rpm and 90 % the loom inserts 720 picks a minute; at 60 picks per inch that is 12 inches of cloth.

questions.q: The 1,440 in 'yards per day = in/min × 1440 ÷ 36' is
options: the number of picks per yard
the number of minutes in 24 hours
the number of inches in 40 yards
questions.explain: 24 × 60 = 1,440 minutes; dividing by 36 converts inches to yards.

questions.q: A-grade fabric is
options: the saleable fabric left after deducting the B-grade percentage
the fabric woven in the first shift
the fabric from the best loom
questions.explain: 480 yards with 1 % B-grade leave 475.2 yards of A-grade; that is what the order is counted in.

questions.q: B-grade fabric consumed no yarn, so it can be ignored when working out yarn for an order.
questions.explain: Rejected metres used warp and weft just like good ones, so the yarn per unit of A-grade fabric is inflated by the B-grade percentage.

questions.q: In the worksheet a 'bag' of yarn is
questions.explain: Warp bags = pounds ÷ 100: 20,000 m × 0.2809 lb/m = 5,617 lb = 56.17 bags.

questions.q: Yarn consumption per unit of fabric includes allowances for
questions.explain: The lecture inflates the bare yarn by contraction and wastage (warp 3 %, weft 5.6 %) and then by the B-grade rejection; efficiency affects speed, not yarn per metre.

questions.q: 'Bags consumed per day (all looms)' is needed by
options: the yarn store, well before the looms start
questions.explain: The lecture notes that the daily bag figure is what the yarn store must plan for in advance (Planning III).

questions.q: A loom running at 800 rpm inserts 800 picks per minute when it is actually running.
questions.explain: One pick per revolution; the efficiency then tells how much of the time it is really running.

questions.q: An efficiency of 90 % means the loom is actually weaving for about
questions.explain: 0.90 × 60 = 54 running minutes an hour; the rest is stops for breaks, weft changes and so on.

questions.q: 'Days to complete' an order is
options: order quantity ÷ (looms × A-grade metres per loom per day)
order quantity × looms ÷ metres per day
questions.explain: 20,000 m ÷ (4 looms × 434.5 m) = 11.5 days. Using only one loom's output ignores the looms allotted.

quizzes.title: Formulas and relationships
quizzes.intro: The production and consumption formulas, and which way they move.

questions.q: Yards per day from inches per minute is
questions.explain: Minutes per day (1,440) then inches to yards (÷ 36): 12 × 1440 ÷ 36 = 480 yd.

questions.q: If the picks per inch are doubled at the same rpm and efficiency, the daily production
questions.explain: Each inch now needs twice as many picks, so the loom makes half as many inches per minute.

questions.q: To turn yards into metres you
questions.explain: A metre is 1.0936 yards, so 475.2 yd ÷ 1.0936 = 434.5 m. Multiplying would make the number bigger.

questions.q: A loom runs at 800 rpm with 90 % efficiency weaving 60 picks per inch. Inches of cloth per minute?
questions.explain: 800 × 0.9 = 720 picks per minute ÷ 60 PPI = 12 in/min.

questions.q: The bare warp yarn in pounds per yard of cloth (before allowances) is
questions.explain: Each end is one yard long per yard of cloth, so total yards = ends; dividing by yards per pound (840 × Ne) gives pounds: 3,780 ÷ 16,800 = 0.225 lb.

questions.q: The length of weft in one yard of cloth, in yards, is
questions.explain: 36 inches of cloth carry PPI × 36 picks, each the reed width in inches long; dividing by 36 converts the total inches to yards — PPI × width.

questions.q: Raising loom efficiency from 80 % to 90 % raises daily production by 12.5 %.
questions.explain: Production is proportional to efficiency: 90 ÷ 80 = 1.125.

questions.q: Yarn per unit of A-grade fabric is higher than yarn per unit of woven fabric because
options: the yarn used in the B-grade metres is spread over the fewer saleable metres
questions.explain: The whole order's yarn is divided by the A-grade output only, so each saleable metre carries a share of the rejected metres' yarn.

questions.q: Changing the weft from Ne 20 to Ne 16 at the same picks and width multiplies the weft pounds per yard by
questions.explain: Coarser yarn has fewer yards per pound (840 × 16 instead of 840 × 20), so the same length weighs 20 ÷ 16 = 1.25 times as much.

questions.q: Halving the picks per inch halves both the daily production and the weft yarn per metre.
questions.explain: Halving PPI doubles production (half the picks per inch of cloth) and halves the weft per metre — they move in opposite directions.

quizzes.title: Worked calculations
quizzes.intro: Loom output and order yarn for the lecture's 20×20/60×60, 63 in construction and nearby cases.

questions.q: A loom at 750 rpm, 85 % efficiency, weaving 50 picks per inch. Inches per minute to two decimals?
A loom makes 12 inches of cloth per minute. Yards per 24-hour day?
480 yards a day with 1 % B-grade. A-grade yards per day to one decimal?
Convert 475.2 yards to metres (1 m = 1.0936 yd), to one decimal.
questions.explain: 475.2 ÷ 1.0936 = 434.5 m of A-grade per loom per day.

questions.q: Construction 20×20/60×60, 63 in: the warp has 60 × 63 = 3,780 ends of Ne 20. Bare warp pounds per yard of cloth, to three decimals?
questions.explain: Yards per pound at Ne 20 = 16,800; 3,780 ÷ 16,800 = 0.225 lb per yard before allowances.

questions.q: A 63 in fabric has 60 picks per inch of Ne 16 weft. Bare weft pounds per yard of cloth, to three decimals?
questions.explain: Weft yards per yard of cloth = 60 × 63 = 3,780; ÷ (840 × 16 = 13,440) = 0.281 lb.

questions.q: An order is 20,000 m and the warp requirement is 0.2809 lb per metre. Warp bags of 100 lb, to two decimals?
20,000 m on 4 looms each giving 434.5 m of A-grade per day. Days to complete, to one decimal?
The order needs 56.17 warp bags and 54.98 weft bags over 11.51 days. Bags consumed per day are about
Bare warp is 0.225 lb/yd. Applying 10 % contraction, 3 % wastage and 1 % B-grade (divide by 0.99), the warp per A-grade yard is about
questions.explain: 0.225 × 1.10 × 1.03 ÷ 0.99 = 0.2575 lb. 0.2318 forgets the contraction; 0.2823 applies the 10 % twice.

quizzes.title: Applied in practice
quizzes.intro: Planning-office decisions: deadlines, loom allotment and what the yarn store must know.

questions.q: A 20,000 m order must ship in 8 days but 4 looms at 434.5 m/day need 11.5 days. The planner should
options: run the looms at a lower PPI
allot 6 looms, which finish in about 7.7 days
reduce the order to A-grade only
questions.explain: 6 × 434.5 = 2,607 m/day → 7.7 days. Lowering PPI changes the fabric the customer ordered.

questions.q: How many looms, each giving 434.5 m of A-grade per day, are needed to finish 20,000 m in 8 days? Round up to whole looms.
questions.explain: 20,000 ÷ (8 × 434.5) = 5.75, so 6 looms must be allotted.

questions.q: If the B-grade rises from 1 % to 5 % on the same looms,
options: A-grade output falls and yarn per A-grade metre rises
the loom speed must be reduced
questions.explain: Fewer saleable metres come from the same woven metres and the same yarn, so both the output and the consumption per good metre move against the mill.

questions.q: The yarn store asks what to stock daily for the 4-loom order using 9.66 bags a day. The sensible instruction is
options: about 10 bags a day, split roughly half warp, half weft
questions.explain: 9.66 rounds to about 10 bags, with warp 56.17 and weft 54.98 almost equal for this square construction.

questions.q: Running the same construction at 1,000 rpm instead of 800 rpm at the same efficiency gives 25 % more fabric per day.
questions.explain: Production is proportional to rpm: 1000 ÷ 800 = 1.25.

questions.q: Warp breaks push the efficiency from 90 % to 70 %. Inches per minute at 800 rpm and 60 PPI become
Yards per day at 800 rpm, 70 % efficiency and 60 picks per inch, to one decimal?
The order needs 56.17 warp bags but the store holds 50. The shortfall to buy is
questions.explain: 56.17 − 50 = 6.17 bags × 100 lb = 617 lb; ordering exactly 6 bags leaves the last 17 lb short.

questions.q: Total yarn for the 20,000 m order is 56.17 + 54.98 = 111.15 bags. The purchase order should be for
questions.explain: Bags come whole, so round up to 112 — rounding down to 111 leaves 15 lb short before any spoilage.

questions.q: Days to complete should be based on A-grade metres per day, not on the grey metres woven.
questions.explain: The order is for saleable fabric, so the worksheet divides 20,000 m by 4 × 434.5 m of A-grade per day.

quizzes.title: Challenge review
quizzes.intro: Harder mixed problems: new constructions, unit slips and consumption for bigger orders.

questions.q: Construction 20×20/72×64, 63 in, on a loom at 700 rpm and 88 % efficiency. Yards per day, to the nearest yard?
That loom makes 385 yd a day with 2 % B-grade. A-grade metres per day (1 m = 1.0936 yd), to one decimal?
A student multiplies 12 in/min by 60 and divides by 36 to get 20 yards per day. The slip is
options: using 60 minutes instead of the 1,440 minutes in a day
questions.explain: 20 yd is the output per hour; per day it is 12 × 1440 ÷ 36 = 480 yd.

questions.q: Warp requirement is 0.2568 lb per yard. Express it per metre (1 m = 1.0936 yd), to four decimals.
questions.explain: A metre is longer than a yard, so the figure rises: 0.2568 × 1.0936 = 0.2809 lb/m.

questions.q: For 20×20/60×60, 63 in the warp and weft bag figures (56.17 and 54.98) are nearly equal because
options: warp and weft have the same count and the same threads per inch
wastage is the same for both
questions.explain: Same Ne 20 and 60 threads per inch each way give the same bare 0.225 lb/yd; only the different contraction and wastage allowances separate them.

questions.q: Six looms each weave 434.5 m of A-grade a day; the order needs 0.2809 lb/m warp and 0.2749 lb/m weft. Bags (100 lb) consumed per day, to two decimals?
A 50,000 m order on 8 looms at 434.5 m/day each takes about
Halving the picks per inch halves the weft yarn needed per metre of cloth.
questions.explain: Weft length per metre is PPI × width, so half the picks means half the weft; the warp per metre is unchanged.

questions.q: Which change both raises daily output and lowers the weft yarn per metre?
questions.explain: Fewer picks per inch speed up the loom's cloth output and cut weft length per metre; efficiency raises output but leaves yarn per metre unchanged.

questions.q: Warp bags of 100 lb for a 50,000 m order at 0.2809 lb per metre, to two decimals?
